newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ex-Nomura chief arrested over racketeer scandal.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nomura chief arrested over racketeer scandal.

text.p: Tokyo prosecutors on Friday arrested former Nomura Securities Co Ltd president Hideo Sakamaki in connection with a widening scandal involving suspected illegal payoffs to a racketeer.

Prosecutors said in a statement that Sakamaki, who stepped down as president in March over the scandal, was suspected of violating the Commercial Code and the Securities and Exchange Law by conspiring with three Nomura executives to pay 38.5 million yen ($331,000) to Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" corporate racketeer at the heart of the affair, in 1995.

The scandal, the second involving Nomura in six years, has not only hurt the brokerage's bottom line but further tarnished the image of Japan's financial institutions as they gear up to compete in Tokyo's increasingly deregulated markets.

The arrest of such a senior figure deals a further hammer blow to Nomura's reputation, as the company had said the scandal was an isolated case of wrongdoing involving only those already arrested in the case.
"The fact that the head (of Nomura) was suspected and arrested is very grave and beyond words," Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters.

Sakamaki, who remained an adviser to the giant brokerage after he stepped down as president, told a parliamentary panel this week that he had briefly met Koike in 1992, but denied knowledge of any stock deals by the racketeer through Nomura.
Sakamaki has said that only two Nomura executives were to blame for the allegedly illegal deals and that the company as a whole was not involved.

Earlier this month Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), filed a complaint with prosecutors against Nomura, two former Nomura executives and a company official alleging they had illegally compensated a firm run by Koike's younger brother, Yoshinori.
Prosecutors then arrested the two former Nomura executives and the company official, as well as the two Koike brothers.

Sokaiya are racketeers who take stakes in companies and extort money from them by threatening to disrupt annual shareholders' meetings or by offering to prevent other shareholders from asking questions.
Payoffs to sokaiya were banned under a revision to the Commercial Code in 1982. Those found to have violated the law face a fine of up to 300,000 yen ($2,586) or up to six months in jail.

Compensation of investors' losses is also banned under the Securities and Exchange Law, which was revised after 1991 scandals at scores of brokerages including Nomura and the other "Big Four" Japanese securities houses.

Prosecutors said on Friday that they believed the cash was handed over on March 15, 1995 as a "token of appreciation" for Koike's future cooperation in helping to ensure the brokerage's annual shareholders' meeting, held the following June, went smoothly.
Prosecutors are also probing one of Japan's biggest banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), in connection with the scandal.

Top DKB executives said last Friday they would step down at the end of June to take responsibility for the bank's improper loans to the younger Koike and his company. They also admitted that the bank might have covered up the deals to the Koike group ahead of Finance Ministry inspections in 1990 and 1994, an act which would violate Japan's Banking Law. ($=116 yen)
